### Greetings from the Center for Augmented Intelligence in Imaging (CAII) of the Department of Radiology, Mayo Clinic, Florida

Greetings from the Center for Augmented Intelligence in Imaging (CAII) of the Department of Radiology, Mayo Clinic, Florida

We welcome you to participate in the “Stroke Thromboembolism Registery of Imaging and Pathology (STRIP) AI Challenge”!
Each year in the United States, over 700,000 individuals experience an ischemic stroke caused by a blood clot blocking an artery to the brain. A second stroke (23% of total events are recurrent) worsens the chances of the patient’s survival. However, subsequent strokes may be mitigated if the source of the thrombotic material can be determined at the time of the first event, thereby directing preventive management of future clot formation and its embolization to brain arteries.

This competition is about predicting the origins of blood clot resulting in ischemic stroke using Digital Pathology Slides (aka Whole Slide Images (WSI)) of the thrombotic material extracted mechanically during acute neurovascular procedures. Collaborative efforts across 18 institutions, led by Waleed Brinjikji, MD of the Mayo Clinic Rochester allowed the compilation of this unique dataset ( <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33722963/)> .
Unlike traditional images, WSIs present many additional challenges due to their high resolution and size. In addition, based on the source MSI scanner hardware, they may be saved in different file formats (e.g., .svs, .ndpi, etc. ). Hence, in order to ease some of the potential pitfalls, we have converted and standardized all collected data into the TIFF format.

You could potentially help many patients by developing and sharing your classification of blood clot origins. We look forward to interacting with you towards this goal.

We hope you will enjoy participating in this competition!

CAII Team, Mayo Clinic Florida

Hosts: Mayo Clinic
Barbaros Selnur Erdal (@Barbaros), Associate Professor of Radiology, Department of Radiology, Mayo Clinic Florida
Mohammed Sobhi Jabal (@Sobhi Jabal), Research Fellow, Department of Radiology, Mayo Clinic Rochester
\*Special thanks to Dr. Waleed Brinjikji, Dr. David F. Kallmes, Dr. Ramanathan Kadirvel, and Dr. Richard D. White.

As far as I have understood there are two ways for reducing computational complexity caused by dataset size:

1) Downscale whole slide images - which will likely result in loss of training signal but you can build and test end to end models faster.
2) Tile creation and selection - in this method you create tiles from images and have criteria for selecting tiles with maximum signal, and then train an MIL based method which is more complicated but may do better (or not, but there's a better chance). Tile creation and selection is key, this will reduce your training time based on pre-selected best guess part of the data.

I have only tried method two and struggled throughout - so that you know how much salt to take these statements with :)

All the best.
